lesson.subject: english
lesson.title: Writing for a Purpose
lesson.summary: Reports, persuasive writing, story mountains and character profiles, playscripts, and editing and reading aloud.
learning_objectives: Write a report and persuasive text
Plan a story with a story mountain and character profile
Edit, improve and read writing aloud

standards.text: Plan, draft, edit and perform writing for different purposes, including reports, persuasion, stories and playscripts

success_criteria: I can write a clear report with headings
I can write persuasively using reasons
I can plan a story and a character
I can edit my writing and read it aloud
lesson.real_life: Writing a school report, a letter to persuade the head teacher and a play for assembly.

blocks.markdown:
Today's big question: how do we choose the right way to write for the right reader?

We will write reports, persuasion, stories and plays.
blocks.say: Welcome back, young author! Today's big question: how do we choose the right way to write for the right reader? A report, a persuasive speech, a story and a play each have their own shape. We will learn them all, then edit and perform our writing. Let's go!

blocks.alt: Writers choose a form to fit their purpose.
blocks.caption: Writers choose a form to fit their purpose.

terms.meaning: The person who writes a book or story.

blocks.markdown:
A **report** gives facts in a clear order, with headings, in the present tense.

Pandas live in the mountains of China. They eat bamboo.
blocks.say: Writers choose their style to fit their purpose. A report gives facts about a topic, clearly and in order. It has a title, an opening that says what it is about, headings for each part, and facts written in the present tense. For example: Pandas live in the mountains of China. A report does not give opinions. Watch how a report is built.

scenes.caption: Title and opening.
scenes.say: First, the title and an opening. All About Pandas. Pandas are large black and white bears.

scenes.caption: Headings and facts.
scenes.say: Then headings for each part, like Where they live and What they eat. Under each heading are facts in the present tense.

question.prompt: Which sentence belongs in a report?
question.explanation: It is a fact in the present tense.

options.text: I think pandas should be everywhere.
Pandas are the cutest animals ever.

blocks.markdown:
**Persuasive writing** tries to convince the reader.

A **power of three** puts three words together: safe, clean and fun.
blocks.say: Persuasive writing tries to convince the reader to agree. It states an opinion, then gives reasons to back it up. A persuasive writer uses strong words, asks questions, and often uses a power of three: three words or phrases together, like safe, clean and fun. Let's persuade someone to recycle.

scenes.caption: Opinion: we should recycle.
scenes.say: The opinion. We should all recycle. A clear opinion at the start.

scenes.caption: Reasons: a power of three.
scenes.say: Now the reasons. Recycling saves energy, protects animals and keeps our streets clean. That is a power of three!

question.prompt: Which is a power of three?
question.hint: How many things are in the list?
question.explanation: Three words together make a power of three.

points: A report gives facts in order, with headings
Persuasive writing gives an opinion backed by reasons and a power of three
blocks.say: Let us remember. A report gives facts in order. Persuasive writing gives an opinion with reasons.

blocks.markdown: A **story mountain** plans the opening, build-up, problem, resolution and ending.
blocks.say: Stories climb like a mountain. At the bottom is the opening, where we meet the characters and setting. Then the build-up, where events begin. At the top is the problem or climax, the most exciting part. Then the resolution, where things are sorted out, and the ending. Planning on a mountain keeps your story shaped.

scenes.caption: Opening.
scenes.say: The opening. Amna and her little brother arrive at the beach. We meet them and the setting.

scenes.caption: Problem at the peak.
scenes.say: The build-up and then the problem at the very top. A huge wave sweeps their kite out to sea.

scenes.caption: Resolution and ending.
scenes.say: Then the resolution. A kind fisherman rescues it, and they all go home happy. That is the ending.

question.prompt: Where is the problem on a story mountain?
question.hint: It is the most exciting part.
question.explanation: The problem or climax is at the peak.

blocks.markdown: A **character profile** describes who a character is, what they like and what they want.
blocks.say: A character profile helps us know a character well before we write. Write their name, age, what they look like, what they like, and one thing they want. Amna is nine. She has bright eyes and a huge laugh. She loves kites. She wants to be brave. Then show it in your writing, rather than telling.

blocks.caption: A profile lists name, age, looks, likes and wants.
blocks.say: Here is a character profile on a card.

blocks.markdown:
A **playscript** has the speaker's name, a colon, then the words.

**Stage directions** go in brackets: (she points at the sea).
blocks.say: A playscript is a story written to be acted. Each speaker's name goes at the start of the line, followed by a colon. No speech marks are needed. Stage directions, which tell the actors what to do, go in brackets. Look at this scene. Amna colon, Look out! The wave is huge! Then in brackets, she points at the sea.

scenes.caption: Amna: Look out! The wave is huge!
scenes.say: Here is a line. Amna, then a colon, then her words. Look out! The wave is huge!

scenes.caption: (She points at the sea.)
scenes.say: A stage direction tells the actor what to do. It goes in brackets, like this: she points at the sea.

blocks.title: Drama pairs
blocks.say: Play the memory game, then think about how you would act a line. Where would you pause? What would your voice sound like?

blocks.say: Let us remember. A playscript has names with colons, and stage directions in brackets.

blocks.markdown:
To **edit** is to read your writing again and make it better.

Check spelling, punctuation, word choices and detail.
blocks.say: Great writing is rarely right the first time. Editors read their work again and make it better. They check spelling and punctuation. They swap dull words for stronger ones. They add detail where a part feels thin. Then they read it aloud to hear the flow. Watch a dull sentence get upgraded.

scenes.caption: Draft: The dog was big and ran.

items.label: The dog was big and ran.

scenes.say: The first draft: The dog was big and ran. It is fine, but dull.

scenes.caption: Edited: The enormous dog sprinted across the field.
scenes.say: The edit: The enormous dog sprinted across the field. Stronger words and more detail.

question.prompt: Which sentence is the better edit?
question.hint: Which has stronger words and detail?
question.explanation: Enormous, sprinted and field give a clearer picture.

options.text: The dog was big and ran.
The enormous dog sprinted across the field.

blocks.markdown: Reading aloud helps us hear the flow of our writing.
blocks.say: The last step is reading aloud. When we hear our writing, we notice clumsy sentences and missing words. Read with expression, pausing at full stops and changing your voice for questions and exclamations. Then make any final fixes.

blocks.alt: Reading aloud shows what to fix.
blocks.caption: Reading aloud shows what to fix.
blocks.say: A writer reading to a friend.

blocks.title: Edit and share
instructions: Read your writing and underline any dull words.
Check spelling and punctuation with a coloured pen.
Read it aloud to a listener and ask for one improvement.
blocks.say: Choose something you wrote earlier. Edit it, then read it to someone and ask for their feedback.
